definition: Feral means wild and untamed, used of a domesticated species that now lives without human contact.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word feral. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know feral should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Three generations after the ranch closed, its horses had gone completely feral and would not let a rider within fifty metres.
A stray is a domestic animal that has wandered off but still seeks people out, while feral goes further and describes animals that have stopped depending on us at all.
Savage is stronger and more judgemental than feral, since it implies ferocity, while a feral goat or cat may simply be shy and self-sufficient.

Untamed means never brought under human control, and it can describe anything from a stallion to a stretch of coastline that people have not mastered. Feral is more particular: a domesticated line that once lived under human care and has since returned to the wild.

Wild describes an animal whose kind was never domesticated in the first place, so it applies to wolves and lynxes but not to runaway livestock. Feral is reserved for species with domestic ancestry -- ranch horses, harbour cats -- now living generation after generation without human contact.

When the last cannery on the harbour shut in 1994, the cats that had lived on its scraps stayed on.
Thirty years and many generations later, the colony under the pier hunts rats at night, dens in the ruined boiler house, and scatters the instant a person steps onto the boards.
The volunteers who leave food there have never touched an adult.
These animals belong to the same species as the tabby asleep on a nearby windowsill, yet they are now entirely feral.
The colony is a domestic species that has lived generations without human contact and bolts from any person, and that return to wildness is what feral means.

Australia now has more camels than any country where camels are native.
They arrived in the 1860s as working animals, shipped in to carry freight across the deserts and handled by drivers every day of their lives.
When railways and motor trucks made the caravans obsolete, the owners simply turned their animals loose.
The descendants of those pack camels are feral: hundreds of thousands of animals breeding in the outback with no human contact at all.
They are not wild in the strict sense, because their ancestors were domesticated; and they are not strays, because they neither seek people nor depend on them.
A century off the lead rope has undone the old arrangement completely.
A stockman who corners one today meets an animal as wary of people as anything the desert has ever produced.
